name: Coffee / green tea ritual

card.summary: Caffeine drinks used as a de-puffing routine; no study has tested the face effect.
card.note: Caffeine affects sleep; high-dose tea extracts linked to liver injury.

quick.overview:
People drink coffee or green tea as a daily ritual intended to reduce puffiness.

Caffeine has a short-lived diuretic effect in non-habitual users, but no published trial has tested these drinks for facial appearance.
quick.mechanism: Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors and may increase urine output briefly; tolerance develops with regular use [2].
quick.risks: Caffeine can disrupt sleep. Concentrated green tea extracts have been associated with liver toxicity [1][2].

lead: The coffee or green tea ritual is a daily habit of drinking a caffeinated beverage, usually in the morning, as part of a routine aimed at looking fresher, more awake and less puffy. Practitioners say the drink helps them look alert, and green tea drinkers add that its polyphenols, chiefly EGCG, fit a skin-friendly diet.[1][2]

Caffeine works mainly by blocking adenosine receptors, which relieves sleepiness. Large single doses can briefly raise urine output in people who have gone without caffeine, while regular drinkers develop tolerance to that effect.[2] This short-lived diuretic action is the basis of the idea that a morning cup reduces facial swelling. A 2014 crossover trial in habitual coffee drinkers found that moderate coffee intake gave hydration comparable to water.[12]

Research on the face-specific claim is absent, but nearby research exists. A 2010 experiment in the BMJ found that photographs of people kept awake for 31 hours were rated as looking less healthy, less attractive and more tired, which is why many people link anything that affects sleep or alertness with appearance.[13] A 2020 cross-sectional survey of Japanese women found that higher coffee and green tea polyphenol intake went with lower scores for facial pigmented spots.[14]

Looks-focused forums discuss caffeine in both directions: some members present coffee as a leanmaxxing and energy aid, while others raise concerns about skin, sleep, hormones and growth.[6][8][10][11] Both drinks are also among the most widely consumed beverages on earth, so the ritual overlaps with ordinary daily life far beyond looksmaxxing.

angle.text: People drink coffee or green tea in the morning to look more awake and to reduce the puffy look they associate with water retention. Green tea drinkers add that its polyphenols fit a skin-friendly diet, and some link the drinks to leaner, more energetic training.

paras: The ritual usually means a cup of coffee or green tea at the start of the day. Brewed green tea is almost entirely water, with caffeine and polyphenols such as EGCG and other catechins; supplements and extracts can contain much higher concentrations, up to about 17 percent caffeine by weight in some extracts.[1] Dried green tea leaf is the richest common dietary source of EGCG, with far less in black tea, because catechins are converted into other compounds during black tea production.[17]

Proponents point to caffeine's alertness effect and to its short-lived diuretic action as reasons the habit might leave the face looking less swollen in the morning. Caffeine's diuretic effect is documented for large doses in people not accustomed to it, and tolerance develops with regular use.[2] Variants practised in appearance circles include black coffee in place of sugary breakfasts, matcha or green tea for those who want less caffeine per cup, and caffeine taken ahead of a workout; some people pair the drink with water, cold splashes or lymphatic massage as a general morning routine.

Green tea is said to have originated in China in the late first millennium BC, and tea seeds reached Japan in the early ninth century. The monk Eisai (1141 to 1215) later promoted tea for health in his 1211 text Kissa Yojoki.[1] Coffee drinking is first reliably reported among Sufi communities in Yemen in the fifteenth century, the first coffeehouse opened in Istanbul in 1555, and the first European coffeehouse outside the Ottoman Empire appeared in Venice in 1647.[16]

Both drinks have long carried health reputations. In the twenty-first century, regulators and reviewers have examined those reputations in detail: a 2011 European Food Safety Authority panel judged most claimed benefits of green tea to lack sufficient scientific support, and in 2015 EFSA published a full opinion setting reference figures for caffeine intake.[1][15] The pairing of caffeine with looks, specifically, is a more recent online development, tied to leanmaxxing and morning-routine content.

Caffeine's structure resembles adenosine, so it occupies adenosine receptors without activating them, which temporarily relieves drowsiness; the A2A receptor appears central to the wakefulness effect.[2] It also inhibits phosphodiesterase and raises dopamine release in parts of the striatum.[2] In the kidney, receptor blockade increases water and salt excretion after large single doses.[2]

EGCG is the most abundant catechin in tea. It is poorly absorbed when swallowed, peaking in blood within a couple of hours, and much of what circulates is in methylated form.[17] Laboratory studies show a range of biological effects, which is the source of the antioxidant reputation tea carries in skincare conversations; the same sources note that these effects have not been demonstrated as benefits in humans.[1][17]

Facial puffiness has many causes, including sleep, salt intake, alcohol, allergies and fluid shifts overnight. The ritual's proponents focus on caffeine's mild diuretic action. EFSA describes caffeine as a mild diuretic.[15] In a counterbalanced crossover trial of 50 healthy male habitual coffee drinkers, about four cups of coffee a day for several days produced total body water, blood markers and 24-hour urine volume similar to a water-only condition, though urinary sodium excretion was higher with coffee. The authors concluded that moderate coffee intake in people used to caffeine hydrates like water; one author is employed by PepsiCo, which the paper discloses.[12]

Caffeine is also used on the skin. Eye creams containing caffeine are sold for puffiness and under-eye circles, and manufacturers cite small studies, often of products that combine several active ingredients, so the effect of caffeine alone is not separated out. No trial of drinking coffee or tea for facial puffiness has been published.

Researchers have examined how sleep shows on the face. In the 2010 Karolinska Institutet experiment, 23 adults aged 18 to 31 were photographed after a normal night and after about 5 hours of sleep followed by 31 hours awake; 65 untrained observers rated the photos. Sleep-deprived faces were rated lower for health and attractiveness and higher for tiredness, and perceived tiredness accounted for much of the drop.[13] The authors noted that real-life interactions might produce larger effects.[13]

This matters to the ritual because caffeine and sleep interact in both directions: people use coffee to feel awake after poor sleep, while caffeine itself can reduce the next night's sleep. A 2023 meta-analysis of 24 studies found that caffeine cut total sleep time by about 45 minutes, sleep efficiency by 7 percent, and added about 9 minutes to the time taken to fall asleep, and it estimated that coffee should be consumed at least 8.8 hours before bedtime to avoid losing sleep time.[3] A 2017 systematic review likewise reported longer sleep latency and worse perceived sleep quality, with large individual differences and genetic variation in sensitivity.[4] Practitioners who value sleep for appearance often respond by moving the cup earlier in the day.

On pigmentation, a 2020 cross-sectional study of 244 healthy Japanese women aged 30 to 60 linked higher total polyphenol intake, largely from coffee (about 53 percent of intake) and green tea (about 8 percent), to lower facial pigmented-spot scores measured by imaging. The design shows association only, intake was self-reported, two authors were employed by companies, and the authors called for longer-term studies.[14]

No studies found on drinking coffee or green tea as a routine for facial puffiness or facial appearance. Research on the drinks themselves covers general health outcomes: a BMJ umbrella review of 201 observational and 17 interventional meta-analyses found coffee consumption more often associated with benefit than harm across many outcomes, with the largest relative risk reductions at three to four cups a day,[5] and Wikipedia reports small blood pressure reductions and modest LDL cholesterol lowering from green tea in trials, including a 2013 Cochrane review, with no good evidence for weight loss.[1]

A 2023 randomized case-crossover trial of 100 adults examined acute effects of caffeinated coffee on heart rhythm, steps, sleep and glucose,[18] and a 2026 JAMA randomized trial examined coffee in people with atrial fibrillation.[19] Studies of green tea and coffee as weight aids are small: a 2023 pilot trial examined coffee and tea in adolescents.[7]

EFSA considers intake up to 400 mg of caffeine per day safe for non-pregnant adults, single doses up to 200 mg unproblematic, and up to 200 mg per day acceptable in pregnancy and breastfeeding. For children and adolescents it proposed 3 mg per kilogram of body weight per day.[15] Health Canada gives the same 400 mg guidance for healthy adults.[2] Even around 100 mg per day can disrupt sleep in some people, and withdrawal symptoms such as headache and fatigue can follow abrupt cessation in regular users.[2][15]

High-dose green tea extract, mainly through EGCG, has been linked to liver damage. EFSA found long-term intake above 800 mg EGCG per day raised liver enzymes in some people, regards traditionally brewed tea as safe with rare liver injury, and in 2017 Health Canada recommended a warning label for extracts.[1][17] A 2020 Cochrane review listed gastrointestinal effects, raised liver enzymes and, less often, insomnia and raised blood pressure among possible adverse effects of extract.[1] Coffee and green tea can also reduce absorption of some medicines; a systematic review reports coffee decreasing levothyroxine absorption, and green tea can interfere with the cancer drug bortezomib.[1][9]

On looksmax.org, caffeine appears in leanmaxxing threads, in supplement stacks and in arguments over whether coffee helps or harms skin, hormones and height. Posts range from enthusiastic (a thread titled 'coffee is so good for leanmaxxing') to cautionary (threads asking whether coffee stunts growth).[6][8][10][11] Some posts argue that caffeine dehydrates the face and works against skincare, while others treat it as a harmless energy source; the debate tends to follow the same lines as the research on tolerance and sleep above.

The wider appearance culture treats morning routines, matcha and green tea powders, and caffeinated skincare as established genres, and many members adopt the drink for its reputation for supporting a lean physique and focused training rather than for the face itself.

lore.intro: Coffee shows up in looksmaxxing forums as a leanmaxxing and energy aid and, in other threads, as something that may harm skin, sleep or growth.[6][10]

claims.believers: Threads on looksmax.org such as one titled 'coffee is so good for leanmaxxing' present caffeine as an appetite and energy aid for getting leaner.[6]
claims.experts: A 2023 pilot study examined coffee and tea consumption and weight control in adolescents,[7] and Wikipedia reports no good evidence that green tea aids weight loss.[1]

claims.claim: A morning cup de-puffs the face.
claims.believers: Practitioners say caffeine's alertness and mild diuretic action leave the face looking less swollen and more awake in the morning.
claims.experts: Caffeine's diuretic effect is documented for large doses in people without tolerance,[2] and a crossover trial found moderate coffee hydrated habitual drinkers like water.[12] No study has tested drinking either beverage for facial puffiness.

claims.claim: Coffee is good for the thyroid.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread titled 'coffee is very good for your thyroid' argues it supports thyroid function.[8]
claims.experts: A systematic review of levothyroxine interactions notes that coffee and other beverages can alter absorption of thyroid medication.[9]

claims.believers: Threads titled 'does coffee stunt your growth' and 'could coffee stunt my growth' show users asking whether caffeine affects height.[10][11]
claims.experts: No study has tested caffeine for effects on height.

claims.claim: Coffee dehydrates and ages facial skin.
claims.believers: Some looksmax.org posters argue caffeine dehydrates the face and works against skincare.
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that the diuretic effect applies to large doses in people without caffeine tolerance, and that regular users do not show increased urine output;[2] the 2014 crossover trial found no dehydration with moderate intake,[12] and a 2020 survey linked higher coffee polyphenol intake with lower pigmented-spot scores.[14]

claims.claim: Green tea polyphenols are good for skin.
claims.believers: Green tea drinkers cite EGCG's antioxidant reputation as part of a skin-friendly diet.
claims.experts: EGCG shows biological effects in laboratory work, but reviews note that most claimed human benefits lacked sufficient support in EFSA's 2011 review;[1][17] a 2020 survey found a weaker, significant link between green tea intake and lower pigmented-spot scores.[14]

claims.claim: Caffeine hurts the looks that sleep builds.
claims.believers: Members who prioritise sleep for appearance say late caffeine costs them the rested look.
claims.experts: A 2023 meta-analysis found caffeine shortened total sleep time by about 45 minutes,[3] and the BMJ 2010 experiment found sleep-deprived faces were rated less healthy and attractive.[13]
